young.html: Plotinus was a teacher who lived in Rome about 1,750 years ago. He loved the ideas of Plato, the great Greek thinker who lived six hundred years before him.

Plotinus pictured all of reality as being like light from the sun. At the center is a perfect source he called the One, or the Good. From it flows everything else, the way light flows from a lamp: first a great Mind, then Soul, then the living world we see. The farther from the source, the dimmer the light. And our souls, he taught, can turn around and travel back toward the light.

young.cap: Tap a ring to read about it. Switch between “going out” and “coming back.”

young.html: The fading light. In a dark room, shine a flashlight at a wall from close up, then step back a few steps at a time. Watch the spot grow bigger and dimmer. Plotinus used light like this as a picture of how everything comes from one source. Talk about it: what is the “source” of good things in your life?
Plotinus was shy about his body and his fame. He would not even let anyone paint his portrait. His friends had an artist come to his lectures and draw him from memory!

full.html: Plotinus (c. AD 204–270) was probably born in Egypt, though he never told even his students where he came from. He studied philosophy in Alexandria for eleven years with a teacher named Ammonius Saccas. Hoping to learn the wisdom of Persia and India, he joined the emperor Gordian III’s army on a campaign to the East, which failed. In AD 244 he settled in Rome and taught there for the rest of his life. The emperor Gallienus admired him, and Plotinus once asked him to rebuild a ruined town in Campania as a “city of philosophers,” Platonopolis, to be run by Plato’s laws. Rivals at court stopped the plan.

His student Porphyry collected his 54 treatises after his death, arranged them in six groups of nine, and published them around AD 300 with a Life of Plotinus. The groups are the Enneads, from the Greek ennea, “nine.” Porphyry put the ethical treatises first, then the world, then the soul, Intellect, and finally the One.

full.text: Is it not enough to carry about this image in which nature has enclosed us? Do you really think I must also consent to leave, as a desirable spectacle to posterity, an image of the image?
full.author: Porphyry
full.work: Life of Plotinus, chapter 1 (Plotinus, refusing to sit for a portrait)
full.ed: Philip Lee Warner, publisher to the Medici Society, London

full.html: Plotinus taught that reality has levels. At the top is the One, which is perfectly simple and beyond anything we can say of it. From the One comes Intellect (nous), a divine Mind that thinks all the Forms, Plato’s eternal patterns. From Intellect comes Soul, which gives life and order to the world of bodies. At the farthest edge is matter, which has no form of its own. Each level flows from the one above without the higher one losing anything, as a fire gives off heat or the sun gives light.

full.html: Two movements: procession, the outflow from the One down to matter, and return, the soul’s turning back. The return is the purpose of philosophy for Plotinus: through virtue, the love of beauty and contemplation, the soul rises to Intellect and, at rare moments, to union with the One.
The treatise On Beauty (Ennead I.6) was the first Plotinus wrote, and the most read. It begins with ordinary beauty and climbs.

full.text: Beauty addresses itself chiefly to sight; but there is a beauty for the hearing too, as in certain combinations of words and in all kinds of music, for melodies and cadences are beautiful; and minds that lift themselves above the realm of sense to a higher order are aware of beauty in the conduct of life, in actions, in character, in the pursuits of the intellect; and there is the beauty of the virtues.
full.author: Plotinus
full.ed: Philip Lee Warner, publisher to the Medici Society, London

full.html: Plotinus then argues against a common view of his day, that beauty is just symmetry, the right proportion of parts. If that were so, he says, a single color or a flash of lightning could not be beautiful, since they have no parts. Beauty, for him, is the presence of form: a thing is beautiful when it shares in an order that comes from above. Near the end he tells the reader how to see the highest beauty.

full.text: Withdraw into yourself and look. And if you do not find yourself beautiful yet, act as does the creator of a statue that is to be made beautiful: he cuts away here, he smoothes there, he makes this line lighter, this other purer, until a lovely face has grown upon his work. So do you also: cut away all that is excessive, straighten all that is crooked, bring light to all that is overcast, labour to make all one glow of beauty and never cease chiselling your statue. … Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
full.author: Plotinus
full.ed: Philip Lee Warner, publisher to the Medici Society, London

full.html: If everything flows from the Good, where does evil come from? Plotinus answers that evil is not a power of its own. It is a lack, like darkness, which is only the absence of light. Matter, at the far edge where form gives out, is the limit of this lack, and the soul goes wrong when it turns its attention away from what is above toward what is below.

Calling Plotinus a “Neoplatonist” as if he thought he was starting something new. The word was invented by modern scholars. Plotinus saw himself as explaining Plato, and he often says his views are only Plato’s, rightly understood.

items: Augustine, two rungs on, read “books of the Platonists” in Latin in Milan, very likely including Plotinus. In the Confessions he says they helped him think of God as spiritual and of evil as a lack of good.
Medieval thought: through Augustine and later writers, Plotinus’s picture of a ladder of being and of light flowing from God shaped Christian, Jewish and Islamic philosophy.
The Renaissance: Marsilio Ficino translated the Enneads into Latin (published 1492), and artists and poets took up Plotinus’s idea of beauty as a trace of a higher world.

deep.text: Context: philosophy as a way to God

deep.html: In the third century the Roman Empire was in crisis: many emperors were killed, the frontiers were attacked and plagues returned. Educated people turned to philosophy and religion for a path to the divine. Plotinus offered one through reason and inner discipline rather than ritual. Porphyry writes that Plotinus reached union with the One four times in the six years Porphyry was with him. These are Plotinus’s beliefs and Porphyry’s report of them; the lesson presents them as such.

items: Is beauty only in the eye of the beholder, or is it something real that we discover?
Can something give without losing anything? What examples can you think of (light, a teacher’s knowledge, a song)?
Is evil a thing in itself, or only the absence of good?
What does it mean to “chisel your own statue”? Is becoming good more like sculpting or like growing?

deep.html: Augustine took up Plotinus’s answer about evil and his inward turn, but placed them within Christian faith in a personal God and in grace. Thomas Aquinas, in the Middle Ages, knew Neoplatonic ideas through Augustine and other writers. Much later, poets of the Romantic era found in Plotinus a philosopher of beauty and of the mind’s ascent.

questions: What is the most beautiful thing you have seen or heard this week? Was it beautiful because of its parts, or something more?
Plotinus would not have his portrait painted. Why might someone not want a picture of himself? Do you agree with him?
What would you “chisel away” from your own statue, if you could?
Plotinus says the eye must become sunlike to see the sun. What do you think he means for people?
Light gets dimmer the farther it travels. Where in life do good things get weaker as they pass from person to person, and where do they get stronger?
